title: 4.3 · Secret messages (Spotting tricks, ciphers)
name: Secret messages (Spotting tricks, ciphers)
summary: Students encode and decode messages with a shift, a keyed substitution and pixels that hide a message in a picture, crack a shift by counting the most common letter, and compare how hard each method is to crack. Then, in Spot the Trick cards 7-10, they catch spoofed senders and ask what a trick message already knew about them. Played in Packet Post. One device per student.
iCan: encode and decode a message with two or more methods
say which method is harder to crack and why
spot a spoofed sender and say what a trick message already knew about me
materials: Cipher Wheels printable (one per student, with a paper fastener)
Trick or Treat cards (for the twin or the block day)
doNow: A message says: You won a free tablet! Reply with your mailbox key to claim it. What do you do? Name two clues that it is a trick.
plan: Explore: a shift on the wheel, then crack one without the key

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 4.2, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 4.2

do: Open Packet Post at Secret Messages on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Level 1 is a shift: turn the wheel 3 and decode the message with the class.
Write KHOOR on the board. Ask the class to crack it without the key by trying shifts one at a time.
say: Encryption scrambles a message so only someone with the key can read it.
Some scrambles are much harder to crack. A shift has only 25 keys to try; a keyed substitution has so many keys that trying them all would take far too long.
ask: How many keys would you have to try to crack a shift? How many would a computer have to try for a keyed substitution?
explore.afterAsk: Take answers. A computer tries all 25 shifts at once. Trying every key is called brute force, and more possible keys is what makes a method strong.
explore.bigIdea: Encryption scrambles a message so only the key opens it, and more possible keys make it harder to crack.

play.stretch: the chapter, then Spot the Trick cards 7-10
play.solo: one device per student; a neighbor may read the message out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: cracking a shift by guessing words instead of counting the most common letter
calling hidden pixels encryption: they hide the message, they do not scramble it
thinking a keyed substitution is just a shift with a bigger number
play.misconception: Hiding a message is not the same as scrambling it: steganography hides it in a picture, encryption makes it unreadable without the key.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Why is a keyed substitution harder than a shift? How many keys would a computer try?
On the trick cards, what did the sender already know about you, and where could they have found it?
showMe: One student cracks a shift on the projector by counting the most common letter; the class predicts the key before the student turns the wheel.

exit.sentencePrompt: Compare two methods from today. Which is harder to crack, and why?
exit.frame: ___ is harder to crack than ___ because ___.

unpluggedTwin.title: Cipher Wheels and Trick or Treat
materials: Cipher Wheels printable and a paper fastener
steps: Students build the wheel and encode a short sentence with a shift; a partner cracks it without the key by counting the most common letter.
They encode the same sentence with the keyed substitution table; the partner tries to crack it and gives up after two minutes.
Compare: how many keys does each method have? Which would a computer crack faster?
Trick cards: for each card, find what the sender already knew about you and where it was public.
Share: what would you keep off a public profile after today?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: a message says you won a free tablet and asks you to reply with your mailbox key. What do you do? Name two clues.

Play Packet Post, chapter Secret Messages, on your own for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 6 2 0 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; sign in with the login cards so the work is saved (signed out is fine only if the cards are missing). No devices or no internet? Run the unplugged twin printed below (Cipher Wheels and Trick or Treat, 15 minutes), then talk about the two discussion questions for 5 minutes.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

add: the Cipher Wheels twin (15 minutes) before Play
10 minutes of the Unit 4 review on Brain Board

notes: The cipher word list is screened at build time; senders on the trick cards are roles, never real names.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: steganography, shift, substitution, spoofing.
Cards 7-10 of Spot the Trick carry the also ids for privacy and public information; they are the stretch.
One device per student at this band.
